name: Straight Line
origin: Jordan Belfort's practitioner sales system, described in his book "Way of the Wolf". This drill is an original training adaptation of its published ideas, not a reproduction of the book or course.
evidenceType: Practitioner system. Built from one seller's experience; not tested in controlled studies. Its author was convicted of securities fraud, so this app teaches only the honest parts: certainty must come from true claims, never from pressure.
fits: Short cycles with a single decision-maker
strains: Long, consensus-driven enterprise cycles with many stakeholders
Buyers who distrust a seller who steers hard
Situations where the honest answer is that the product is not a fit
coreMoves: Take control early: state who you are, why you are calling and where the call is going in the first 15 seconds.
Come across as sharp, enthusiastic and expert from the first sentence. Energy and clarity, not hype.
Use deliberate tonality and pacing: slow down for important points, sound curious when asking, certain when stating facts.
Qualify with ordered questions before pitching: is there a need, is there budget, is this the decision-maker, what is the timeline.
Build the buyer's certainty on three scales at once: the product, you, and your company.
Treat an objection as a sign of uncertainty on one of the three scales. Acknowledge it, then loop back to rebuild certainty on that scale instead of arguing the objection head-on.
Lower the effort of saying yes (small, clear next step) and make the true cost of the status quo visible.

opener: Took control in the first 15 seconds with a clear reason for the call
Sounded sharp and credible rather than scripted or apologetic
Asked permission or set an agenda instead of launching into a pitch
discovery: Asked qualifying questions in a sensible order before pitching
Confirmed need, authority, budget and timeline
Kept the conversation moving toward a decision without rushing past answers
objectionHandling: Identified which certainty scale (product, rep, company) the objection came from
Acknowledged the objection, then looped back to rebuild certainty with true, specific evidence
Did not argue head-on or repeat the same pitch louder
close: Asked for a specific, low-effort next step
Made the cost of doing nothing concrete and honest
Accepted a clear no instead of pushing past it

ethicsGuardrails: Certainty must come from accurate claims. Inflating results to build certainty is deception.
Looping is allowed at most twice on the same objection; after a clear no, the rep must stop.
No invented urgency or fake 'today only' terms.
